To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

population connectivity for three Great Plains species is most sensitive to landscape conditions in the northern Great Plains and that connectivity for species with different dispersal abilities is not necessarily correlated across the region.

population connectivity is predicted to be most sensitive to landscape resistance in areas with the highest habitat quality, and that landscape resistance is most important for species with the greatest dispersal ability.

Connectivity for species of conservation interest in the Great Plains is more sensitive to variation in landscape resistance for species with high dispersal abilities than for species with low dispersal abilities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of a new analytical approach for predicting the effects of landscape conditions and species traits on population connectivity at continental scales.
the development of a spatially explicit, quantitative approach to conservation planning that can be used to predict the effects on population connectivity of landscape change.

understanding the effects of landscape structure on population connectivity for species with disparate life history traits and distributions, and the application of these results to conservation planning and management.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the connectivity analysis presented in this paper has provided valuable information on population connectivity across the American Great plains.
the connectivity of swift fox, massasauga, and lesser prairie-chickens is highly sensitive to landscape conditions, particularly the presence of roads.

the results indicate that connectivity for all three species of conservation concerns in the American Great plains is highly sensitive to the dispersal ability of the species, and the landscape conditions in the area.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
connectivity is sensitive to landscape structure, and that landscape conditions are not uniform across the study area, but vary with respect to the species’ dispersal abilities.
connectivity is sensitive to landscape resistance and species dispersal, and that connectivity is a function of the species’ distribution and the distribution of landscape resistance.
the Great Plains region has the potential to be a highly connected landscape, especially for species with high dispersal abilities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Great Plains region has high connectivity potential for swift fox, but lower connectivity for the other two species.
connectivity analyses can be used to identify the location of critical habitats, corridors, barriers and gaps in the landscape.
the spatial extent of the Great Plains region is too large for conservation efforts to be successful unless they consider connectivity across large spatial extents.
